claim: IL-1R8 KO hippocampal neurons display an increased number of immature, thin spines compared to WT neurons.
source: Compared to their WT counterpart, IL-1R8 KO neurons displayed an increased number of immature, thin spines and a decreased number of mature, mushroom spines (Figure 1A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1A-C and stated in the text.

claim: IL-1R8 KO hippocampal neurons display a decreased number of mature, mushroom spines compared to WT neurons.
source: Compared to their WT counterpart, IL-1R8 KO neurons displayed an increased number of immature, thin spines and a decreased number of mature, mushroom spines (Figure 1A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1A-C and stated in the text.

claim: IL-1R8 KO neurons have significantly reduced spine width compared to WT neurons.
source: along with a significant reduction of spine width (Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PSD-95 puncta density is significantly lower in IL-1R8 KO neurons compared to WT neurons.
source: Also PSD-95 puncta density (Figure 1E) and size (Figure 1F) were significantly lower in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PSD-95 puncta size is significantly lower in IL-1R8 KO neurons compared to WT neurons.
source: Also PSD-95 puncta density (Figure 1E) and size (Figure 1F) were significantly lower in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The levels of the postsynaptic protein PSD-95 are significantly reduced in IL-1R8 KO neuronal cultures.
source: Consistently, the levels of the postsynaptic protein PSD-95, evaluated by western blotting of culture homogenates were significantly reduced (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) is significantly reduced in IL-1R8 deficient cultures.
source: In line with a synaptic defect, patch clamp recording of IL-1R8 deficient cultures revealed that the frequency, but not the amplitude, of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) was significantly reduced (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1I-K.

claim: The amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) is not significantly different in IL-1R8 deficient cultures compared to WT.
source: In line with a synaptic defect, patch clamp recording of IL-1R8 deficient cultures revealed that the frequency, but not the amplitude, of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) was significantly reduced (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1I-K.

claim: Spine defects are detected in CA1 pyramidal neurons of IL-1R8 KO mice compared to WT controls.
source: Spine defects (Figure 2A and B) and reduction in synaptic markers (Figure 2C and D) were also detected in CA1 pyramidal neurons of IL1R8 KO mice with respect to age-matched WT controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by Golgi staining data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Reduction in synaptic markers is detected in CA1 pyramidal neurons of IL-1R8 KO mice compared to WT controls.
source: Spine defects (Figure 2A and B) and reduction in synaptic markers (Figure 2C and D) were also detected in CA1 pyramidal neurons of IL1R8 KO mice with respect to age-matched WT controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: WT neurons undergo chemical LTP as evidenced by increased density of PSD-95-positive puncta and mushroom spines.
source: Under these conditions, a significant increase in the density of both PSD-95-positive puncta and mushroom spines occurred in WT but not in IL-1R8 KO neurons (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: IL-1R8 KO neurons do not undergo chemical LTP as evidenced by lack of increase in density of PSD-95-positive puncta and mushroom spines.
source: Under these conditions, a significant increase in the density of both PSD-95-positive puncta and mushroom spines occurred in WT but not in IL-1R8 KO neurons (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: No increase in mEPSC amplitude and frequency is recorded over time in IL-1R8 KO neurons following LTP induction.
source: Similarly, no increase in mEPSC amplitude and frequency was recorded over time in IL-1R8 KO neurons (Figure 3D–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Hippocampal IL-1R8 KO neurons are unable to undergo synaptic plasticity.
source: univocally indicating that hippocampal IL-1R8 KO neurons are unable to undergo synaptic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined structural and functional LTP data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Double IL-1R8 KO IL-1R KO neurons display an increase in mushroom spine density compared to WT neurons.
source: Double IL-1R8 KO IL-1R KO neurons displayed an increase in mushroom spine density (number of spines/micron, mean ± SEM, WT: 0,1581 ± 0,01508, n = 32; IL-1R8 KO IL-1R KO: 0,2585 ± 0,0154, n = 41, Student t test, p<0,0001)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative spine density measurements.

claim: Double IL-1R8 KO IL-1R KO neurons show enhanced mEPSC frequency compared to WT neurons.
source: accompanied by enhanced mEPSCs frequency and amplitude (mEPSC frequency, mean ± SEM, WT: 1317 ± 0,1714, n = 12; IL-1R8 KO IL-1R KO: 2432 ± 0,3187, n = 17, Student t test, p<0,05
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: IL-1R signaling plays a role in controlling synaptic structure and function.
source: These data suggest a role for IL-1R signaling in controlling synaptic structure and function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue of synaptic defects in double IL-1R8 KO IL-1R KO neurons.

claim: IL1Ra treatment increases mushroom spine density in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
source: hippocampal neurons from IL-1R8 KO mice exposed overnight to IL1Ra (Anakinra), a naturally-occurring IL-1 receptor antagonist (Dinarello, 2009), displayed increased density of both mushroom spines (Figure 4A and B) and PSD-95 puncta (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: IL1Ra treatment increases PSD-95 puncta density in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
source: hippocampal neurons from IL-1R8 KO mice exposed overnight to IL1Ra (Anakinra), a naturally-occurring IL-1 receptor antagonist (Dinarello, 2009), displayed increased density of both mushroom spines (Figure 4A and B) and PSD-95 puncta (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: IL1Ra-treated IL-1R8 KO neurons recover their ability to undergo structural LTP.
source: Furthermore, IL1Ra-treated neurons from IL-1R8 KO mice recovered their ability to undergo both structural and functional LTP, as indicated by the increased density of spines and PSD-95 (Figure 4A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: IL1Ra-treated IL-1R8 KO neurons recover their ability to undergo functional LTP as indicated by increased mEPSC frequency and amplitude.
source: Furthermore, IL1Ra-treated neurons from IL-1R8 KO mice recovered their ability to undergo both structural and functional LTP, as indicated by the increased density of spines and PSD-95 (Figure 4A–C) and mEPSC frequency and amplitude (Figure 4D–F) following the application of the c-LTP protocol.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The IL-1R8 KO synaptic phenotype results from hyperactivation of the IL-1R pathway as a result of IL-1R8 silencing.
source: Therefore, the IL-1R8 KO synaptic phenotype results from hyperactivation of the IL-1R pathway as a result of IL-1R8 silencing.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments with IL1Ra and double knockout data.

claim: Overnight treatment of WT neurons with IL-1β results in an increased number of immature thin spines.
source: Consistently, pharmacological activation of IL-1R pathway in WT neurons through overnight treatment with IL-1β (40 ng/ml for 14 hr) resulted in an increased number of immature thin spines and a decreased number of mature mushroom-type spines (Figure 4G–I)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: Overnight treatment of WT neurons with IL-1β results in a decreased number of mature mushroom-type spines.
source: Consistently, pharmacological activation of IL-1R pathway in WT neurons through overnight treatment with IL-1β (40 ng/ml for 14 hr) resulted in an increased number of immature thin spines and a decreased number of mature mushroom-type spines (Figure 4G–I)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: Overnight treatment of WT neurons with IL-1β results in decreased PSD-95 puncta density.
source: Consistently, pharmacological activation of IL-1R pathway in WT neurons through overnight treatment with IL-1β (40 ng/ml for 14 hr) resulted in an increased number of immature thin spines and a decreased number of mature mushroom-type spines (Figure 4G–I) and PSD-95 puncta (Figure 4G and J)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4G and J.

claim: IL-1β treatment prevents WT neurons from undergoing synaptic potentiation.
source: accompanied by inability to undergo LTP (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4G-J.

claim: Exposure of WT neurons to IL-1Ra prevents LTP as assessed by confocal analysis.
source: Of note, exposure of WT neurons to IL-1Ra prevented LTP, as assessed by confocal analysis (Figure 4A–C) or electrophysiological recording (Figure 4D–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Exposure of WT neurons to IL-1Ra prevents LTP as assessed by electrophysiological recording.
source: Of note, exposure of WT neurons to IL-1Ra prevented LTP, as assessed by confocal analysis (Figure 4A–C) or electrophysiological recording (Figure 4D–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: IL-1R acts positively in supporting LTP even when IL-1R8 expression is not perturbed.
source: indicating that IL-1R acts positively in supporting LTP, even when IL-1R8 expression is not perturbed.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that IL-1Ra prevents LTP in WT neurons.

claim: Neurons genetically devoid of IL-1 receptor (IL-1R KO) are unable to undergo plasticity phenomena.
source: In line with these observations, we found that neurons genetically devoid of IL-1 receptor (IL-1R KO) were unable to undergo plasticity phenomena (mushroom spine density: WT, no LTP: 0,13 ± 0009, n = 19; WT, + LTP: 0,36 ± 0,03, n = 18; Student t test, p<00001. IL-1R KO, no LTP: 0,41 ± 0,03; IL-1R KO, + LTP: 0,49 ± 0,03 n = 18; Student t test, p ns = 0,1024).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative spine density measurements.

claim: Either pharmacological or genetic silencing of IL-1R is sufficient to alter dendritic spine morphology and plasticity.
source: Therefore, in line with literature data (Costello et al., 2011; Schneider et al., 1998; Coogan and O'Connor, 1999; Avital et al., 2003), either pharmacological or genetic silencing of IL-1R is per se sufficient to alter dendritic spine morphology and plasticity
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Physiological levels of IL-1R activation are required for correct long-term potentiation.
source: indicating that physiological levels of IL-1R activation are required for correct long-term potentiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both excess and deficiency of IL-1R activity impair LTP.

claim: Treatment of WT mice with IL-1β leads to transcriptional alterations in 1084 genes.
source: Treatment of WT mice with IL-1β led to transcriptional alterations in 1084 genes (60.6% downregulated and 39.4% upregulated, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 60.6% of genes altered by IL-1β treatment in WT mice are downregulated.
source: Treatment of WT mice with IL-1β led to transcriptional alterations in 1084 genes (60.6% downregulated and 39.4% upregulated, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 39.4% of genes altered by IL-1β treatment in WT mice are upregulated.
source: Treatment of WT mice with IL-1β led to transcriptional alterations in 1084 genes (60.6% downregulated and 39.4% upregulated, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: IL-1R8 KO mice show alterations in expression of 639 genes compared to WT.
source: IL-1R8 KO mice showed alterations in expression of 639 genes compared to WT (49.1% downregulated and 50.9% upregulated, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 49.1% of genes altered in IL-1R8 KO mice are downregulated.
source: IL-1R8 KO mice showed alterations in expression of 639 genes compared to WT (49.1% downregulated and 50.9% upregulated, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 50.9% of genes altered in IL-1R8 KO mice are upregulated.
source: IL-1R8 KO mice showed alterations in expression of 639 genes compared to WT (49.1% downregulated and 50.9% upregulated, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: There is a highly significant overlap of 193 genes whose expression is altered by either IL-1β treatment or IL-1R8 deficiency.
source: Comparing the two sets of genes, we observed a highly significant overlap of 193 genes whose expression was altered by either IL-1β treatment and IL-1R8 deficiency (Fischer's exact test; P value = 2.2e-16; Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.95; 61.7% downregulated and 38.3% upregulated, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and statistical analysis.

claim: The deregulated genes in IL-1β-treated and IL-1R8 KO mice are clustered in specific categories referring to biological processes such as hippocampal development and synaptic transmission.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that the deregulated genes are clustered in specific categories referring to biological processes such as hippocampal development and synaptic transmission, among others (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Anakinra treatment largely reverses the transcriptional alterations observed in IL-1R8 KO mice (83.1% at FDR <0.1).
source: Moreover, consistent with our results in neuronal cultures, transcriptomic analysis of IL-1R8 KO mice treated with Anakinra revealed that this pharmacological treatment largely reversed the transcriptional alterations observed in IL-1R8 KO mice (83.1%; False Discovery Rate/FDR <0.1; 80.8%, FDR < 0.05)
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing IL-1R8 KO mice with and without Anakinra treatment.

claim: Anakinra treatment reverses most of the shared changed genes between IL-1R8 KO mice and IL1β stimulated mice (89.0% at FDR <0.1).
source: including most of the shared changed genes between IL-1R8 KO mice and in IL1β stimulated mice (89.0%; FDR < 0.1; 88.7%, FDR < 0.05) (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Anakinra reverses the downregulation of important synaptic genes such as Mdga1 in IL-1R8 KO mice.
source: Notably, the reversion affected important synaptic genes downregulated in both IL-1R8 KO and IL-1β-treated mice, such as Mdga1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), Cnih2 and Sez6 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acute IL-1β treatment and IL-1R8 deficiency trigger overlapping gene programs which are reversed by acute exposure to Anakinra in IL-1R8 KO mice.
source: These data indicate that acute IL-1β treatment and IL-1R8 deficiency trigger overlapping gene programs which are reversed, in the case of IL-1R8 KO mice, by acute exposure to Anakinra.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the transcriptomic analysis results.

claim: Overnight treatment of IL-1R8 KO neurons with rapamycin reverses the defective spine phenotype.
source: Overnight treatment of 15 DIV IL-1R8 KO neurons with 20 nM rapamycin (Vézina et al., 1975), which inhibits both mTORC1 and mTORC2, was sufficient to reverse the defective spine phenotype, with IL-1R8 KO treated neurons displaying an increase in density of both mushroom spines (Figure 6A and B) and PSD-95 puncta (Figure 6A and C) relative to untreated IL-1R8 KO neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A-C and cited literature.

claim: Overnight exposure to LY294002 rescues mushroom spine density in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
source: Similarly, overnight exposure to 30 μM LY294002, a specific inhibitor of PI3K, or 20 nM wortmannin, a PI3-K/Akt signal transduction inhibitor, rescued mushroom spine and PSD-95 densities in IL-1R8 KO neurons (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Overnight exposure to wortmannin rescues mushroom spine density in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
source: Similarly, overnight exposure to 30 μM LY294002, a specific inhibitor of PI3K, or 20 nM wortmannin, a PI3-K/Akt signal transduction inhibitor, rescued mushroom spine and PSD-95 densities in IL-1R8 KO neurons (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Hyperactivation of IL-1R in IL-1R8 KO neurons impairs spine morphogenesis and plasticity through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway.
source: These data demonstrate that hyperactivation of IL-1R in IL-1R8 KO neurons impairs spine morphogenesis and plasticity through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments with PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway inhibitors.

claim: Treatment with rapamycin, LY294002, and wortmannin restores the neuronal ability to sustain LTP in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
source: Consistent with the involvement of mTOR in the IL-1R8 KO neuron defects, treatment with the PI3 kinase inhibitors, LY294002 and wortmannin restored the neuronal ability to sustain LTP. Moreover, specific inhibition of mTOR by the drug rapamycin rescues synaptic morphology in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments with pathway inhibitors.

claim: The PI3K-regulated pathway is involved in the downstream signaling that connects excessive IL-1R activation to the morphological and functional impairments of dendritic spines in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
source: These results indicate that the PI3K-regulated pathway is involved in the downstream signaling that connects excessive IL-1R activation to the morphological and functional impairments of dendritic spines observed in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments with PI3K inhibitors.

claim: IL-1R8 KO hippocampal cultures have higher levels of MeCP2 protein compared to controls.
source: Western blotting and immunofluorescence analysis of MeCP2 in IL-1R8 KO hippocampal cultures revealed higher levels of the protein with respect to controls (Figure 7A and B)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: There are no differences in MeCP2 transcript levels between WT and IL-1R8 KO neurons.
source: in the absence of differences in the transcript levels (normalized counts WT = 4857 ± 97.46, WT+IL1β = 4936 ± 281.3, IL-1R8 KO = 4864 ± 201.7, IL-1R8 KO+Anakinra = 3599 ± 232.6, mean ± SEM, p>0,05, one-way ANOVA, Tukey's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Overnight treatment of IL-1R8 KO neurons with IL1Ra normalizes MeCP2 levels.
source: Indeed, overnight treatment of IL-1R8 KO neurons with either IL1Ra (20 or 100 ng/ml) or rapamycin (20 nM) resulted in the normalization of MeCP2 levels, as assessed by Western Blotting (Figure 7A and B) or immunofluorescence (Figure 7C and D)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Overnight treatment of IL-1R8 KO neurons with rapamycin normalizes MeCP2 levels.
source: Indeed, overnight treatment of IL-1R8 KO neurons with either IL1Ra (20 or 100 ng/ml) or rapamycin (20 nM) resulted in the normalization of MeCP2 levels, as assessed by Western Blotting (Figure 7A and B) or immunofluorescence (Figure 7C and D)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: MeCP2 is increased in IL-1R8 KO neurons as a consequence of the hyperactivation of IL-1R and downstream to the mTOR pathway.
source: thus indicating that MeCP2 is increased in IL-1R8 KO neurons as a consequence of the hyperactivation of IL-1R and downstream to the mTOR pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments with IL1Ra and rapamycin.

claim: MeCP2 levels are increased by immunofluorescence in cultured WT neurons exposed to IL-1β.
source: Finally MeCP2 levels were increased by immunofluorescence (Figure 7E and F) and by western blotting (Figure 7G and H) also in cultured WT neurons exposed to IL-1β (40 ng/ml for 14 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: MeCP2 levels are increased by western blotting in cultured WT neurons exposed to IL-1β.
source: Finally MeCP2 levels were increased by immunofluorescence (Figure 7E and F) and by western blotting (Figure 7G and H) also in cultured WT neurons exposed to IL-1β (40 ng/ml for 14 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: MeCP2 levels are significantly lower in both hippocampus and cortex of adult IL-1R KO mice compared to WT.
source: Consistently, MeCP2 levels, analyzed by Western Blotting, were significantly lower in both hippocampus and cortex of adult IL-1R KO mice (7 months old) (normalized integrated density of MeCP2 levels in hippocampus, WT: 1 ± 0,0535 (n = 5); IL-1R KO: 0795 ± 0,0121 (n = 5), Student t test, p<0,01. Normalized integrated density of MeCP2 levels in cortex, WT: 1 ± 0,0586 (n = 5); IL-1R KO: 0,7792 ± 0,0473 (n = 5), Student t test, p<0005).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data.

claim: Silencing MeCP2 in IL-1R8 KO neurons reverses the morphological phenotype.
source: While WT neurons with silenced MeCP2 showed abnormal spine morphology, with a decreased density of mushroom spines (Figure 8C and D) and PSD95 puncta (Figure 8C and E), IL-1R8 KO neurons with silenced MeCP2 reverted the morphological phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8C-E.

claim: MeCP2 silenced IL-1R8 KO neurons rescue their ability to undergo LTP.
source: Even more interestingly, MeCP2 silenced neurons rescued their ability to undergo LTP (Figure 8F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 8F-H.

claim: Recovery of MeCP2 to control levels is sufficient to acutely rescue the synaptic defects observed in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
source: Therefore, recovery of MeCP2 to control levels is sufficient to acutely rescue the synaptic defects observed in IL-1R8 KO neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MeCP2 silencing rescue experiments.

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis reveals significantly higher expression of MeCP2 in IL-1R8 KO neurons in hippocampus (CA1 region) compared to WT.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis of hippocampus (CA1 region) and cortex revealed a significantly higher expression of MeCP2 in IL-1R8 KO neurons compared to WT, as indicated by the quantitation of the MeCP2 integrated density value per neuron and the cumulative distribution of neuronal integrated density values (Figure 9A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9A-E.

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis reveals significantly higher expression of MeCP2 in IL-1R8 KO neurons in cortex compared to WT.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis of hippocampus (CA1 region) and cortex revealed a significantly higher expression of MeCP2 in IL-1R8 KO neurons compared to WT, as indicated by the quantitation of the MeCP2 integrated density value per neuron and the cumulative distribution of neuronal integrated density values (Figure 9A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9A-E.

claim: Western blot analysis reveals higher levels of MeCP2 in the hippocampus of IL-1R8 KO mice compared to WT.
source: Consistently, western blot analysis of either hippocampus or cortex revealed higher levels of MeCP2 in the brains of IL-1R8 KO mice (Figure 9F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 9F-H.

claim: Western blot analysis reveals higher levels of MeCP2 in the cortex of IL-1R8 KO mice compared to WT.
source: Consistently, western blot analysis of either hippocampus or cortex revealed higher levels of MeCP2 in the brains of IL-1R8 KO mice (Figure 9F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 9F-H.

claim: Administration of 30 mg/kg Anakinra to IL-1R8 KO mice for three consecutive days significantly reduces MeCP2 protein in hippocampus.
source: Notably, administration of 30 mg/kg Anakinra to IL-1R8 KO mice for three consecutive days significantly reduced MeCP2 protein (Figure 9F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 9F-H.

claim: Administration of 30 mg/kg Anakinra to IL-1R8 KO mice for three consecutive days significantly reduces MeCP2 protein in cortex.
source: Notably, administration of 30 mg/kg Anakinra to IL-1R8 KO mice for three consecutive days significantly reduced MeCP2 protein (Figure 9F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 9F-H.

claim: Higher levels of MeCP2 are detectable in the brain of IL-1R8 KO mice.
source: These data indicate that higher levels of MeCP2 are detectable in the brain of IL-1R8 KO mice and that the acute inhibition of IL-1R by Anakinra reduces hippocampal and cortical MeCP2 levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical and western blotting data.

claim: Acute inhibition of IL-1R by Anakinra reduces hippocampal and cortical MeCP2 levels in IL-1R8 KO mice.
source: These data indicate that higher levels of MeCP2 are detectable in the brain of IL-1R8 KO mice and that the acute inhibition of IL-1R by Anakinra reduces hippocampal and cortical MeCP2 levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data.

claim: Treatment with glycyrrhizic acid ameliorates the spatial memory impairment of IL-1R8 KO mice in the novel place recognition test.
source: To this aim IL-1R8 KO mice were analyzed for novel place recognition test three days after the treatment with the anti-inflammatory compound glycyrrhizic acid (50 mg/kg), which binds to high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) protein and inhibits IL-1 activity (Sakamoto et al., 2001; Mollica et al., 2007) or with 30 mg/kg Anakinra. Both treatments ameliorated the spatial memory impairment of IL-1R8 KO mice (Figure 10A)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 10A and cited literature.

claim: Treatment with Anakinra ameliorates the spatial memory impairment of IL-1R8 KO mice in the novel place recognition test.
source: To this aim IL-1R8 KO mice were analyzed for novel place recognition test three days after the treatment with the anti-inflammatory compound glycyrrhizic acid (50 mg/kg), which binds to high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) protein and inhibits IL-1 activity (Sakamoto et al., 2001; Mollica et al., 2007) or with 30 mg/kg Anakinra. Both treatments ameliorated the spatial memory impairment of IL-1R8 KO mice (Figure 10A)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: 50% of IL-1R8 KO mice display a significantly improved discrimination index after Anakinra treatment.
source: with 50% IL-1R8 KO mice displaying a significantly improved discrimination index after Anakinra treatment (p=0,0168 paired Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data.

claim: The rewarded T-maze reveals an impairment of spatial memory in IL-1R8 KO mice.
source: In line with the concept that alternation, either rewarded or spontaneous, detects hippocampal dysfunction even better than the Morris water maze (reviewed in Deacon and Rawlins, 2006), the rewarded T-maze (Figure 10C), but not the Morris water maze (Figure 10B), revealed an impairment of spatial memory in IL-1R8 KO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 10C and cited literature.

claim: The Morris water maze does not reveal an impairment of spatial memory in IL-1R8 KO mice.
source: In line with the concept that alternation, either rewarded or spontaneous, detects hippocampal dysfunction even better than the Morris water maze (reviewed in Deacon and Rawlins, 2006), the rewarded T-maze (Figure 10C), but not the Morris water maze (Figure 10B), revealed an impairment of spatial memory in IL-1R8 KO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 10B and cited literature.

claim: Treatment with Anakinra ameliorates the performance of IL-1R8 KO mice in the rewarded T-maze.
source: Treatment with Anakinra ameliorated the performance (Figure 10C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: IL-1R8 KO mice perform a significantly higher number of errors during the acquisition phase compared to WT mice.
source: Consistent with these data, IL-1R8 KO mice performed a significantly higher number of errors during the acquisition phase with respect to WT and Anakinra-treated IL-1R8 KO mice (Figure 10D).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Anakinra-treated IL-1R8 KO mice perform a significantly lower number of errors during the acquisition phase compared to untreated IL-1R8 KO mice.
source: Consistent with these data, IL-1R8 KO mice performed a significantly higher number of errors during the acquisition phase with respect to WT and Anakinra-treated IL-1R8 KO mice (Figure 10D).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: WT mice treated with Anakinra display impaired spatial memory in the rewarded T-maze.
source: Interestingly, also WT mice treated with Anakinra displayed impaired spatial memory (Figure 10C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Anakinra ameliorates the spatial memory of IL-1R8 KO mice.
source: These data indicate that Anakinra ameliorates the spatial memory of IL-1R8 KO mice and confirm that blockade of IL-1R originates learning defects in WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from multiple tests.

claim: Blockade of IL-1R originates learning defects in WT mice.
source: These data indicate that Anakinra ameliorates the spatial memory of IL-1R8 KO mice and confirm that blockade of IL-1R originates learning defects in WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data showing impairment in WT mice treated with Anakinra.

claim: Hyperactivation of the interleukin 1 pathway through ablation of IL-1R8 leads to up-regulation of the mTOR pathway.
source: Here we show that hyperactivation of the interleukin 1 pathway, through either ablation of the interleukin 1 receptor 8 (IL-1R8, also known as SIGIRR or Tir8) or activation of IL-1R, leads to up-regulation of the mTOR pathway and increased levels of the epigenetic regulator MeCP2
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: This study links neuronal MeCP2 to immune activation for the first time.
source: By linking for the first time neuronal MeCP2, a key player in brain development, to immune activation and demonstrating that synaptic defects can be pharmacologically reversed, these data open the possibility for novel treatments of neurological diseases through the immune system modulation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a novel finding of the study.

claim: Synaptic defects caused by IL-1R8 deficiency can be pharmacologically reversed.
source: By linking for the first time neuronal MeCP2, a key player in brain development, to immune activation and demonstrating that synaptic defects can be pharmacologically reversed, these data open the possibility for novel treatments of neurological diseases through the immune system modulation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by Anakinra treatment experiments.

claim: IL-1β impairs BDNF-induced expression of molecules critical for activity-dependent synaptic plasticity, including CREB, Arc, and cofilin.
source: IL-1β was found to impair brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-induced expression of molecules critical for activity-dependent synaptic plasticity, including cAMP response element binding protein (CREB), Arc, and cofilin, thus reducing actin polymerization and impairing spine morphogenesis (Tong et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tong et al., 2012.

claim: IL-1β reduces actin polymerization and impairs spine morphogenesis.
source: IL-1β was found to impair brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-induced expression of molecules critical for activity-dependent synaptic plasticity, including cAMP response element binding protein (CREB), Arc, and cofilin, thus reducing actin polymerization and impairing spine morphogenesis (Tong et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tong et al., 2012.

claim: IL-1β controls different neuronal functions, including excitability and transmitter release, via multiple biochemical pathways.
source: In addition, IL-1β controls different neuronal functions, including excitability and transmitter release, via multiple biochemical pathways (Weber et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Weber et al., 2010.

claim: IL-1R8-deficient mice are impaired in novel object recognition, spatial reference memory and long-term potentiation.
source: Notably, IL-1R8-deficient mice are impaired in novel object recognition, spatial reference memory and long-term potentiation (LTP), defects that occur in the absence of any external inflammatory stimuli (Costello et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Costello et al., 2011.

claim: The defects in IL-1R8-deficient mice occur in the absence of any external inflammatory stimuli.
source: Notably, IL-1R8-deficient mice are impaired in novel object recognition, spatial reference memory and long-term potentiation (LTP), defects that occur in the absence of any external inflammatory stimuli (Costello et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Costello et al., 2011.

claim: IL-1R8 has been previously reported to regulate mTOR kinase activity in Th17 cells.
source: IL-1R8 has been previously reported to regulate mTOR kinase activity in Th17 cells, playing a nonredundant role in controlling mTOR-dependent differentiation, proliferation and cytokine production (Gulen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gulen et al., 2010.

claim: The mTOR pathway is closely linked to ILR/TLR signaling since PI3 kinase is required for activation of NF-κB by IL-1.
source: Remarkably, the mTOR pathway is closely linked to ILR/TLR signaling since PI3 kinase is required for activation of NF-κB by IL-1 (Gulen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gulen et al., 2010.

claim: The signaling module containing MyD88, phosphorylated IRAK and TRAF6 is essential for PI3K recruitment and Akt activation.
source: Furthermore, the signaling module containing the MyD88 adaptor protein, together with phosphorylated IRAK and TRAF6, which is downstream to both IL-1R and TLRs activation, is essential for PI3K recruitment and Akt activation, making mTOR one of the downstream targets of ILR/TLRs signaling (Gulen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gulen et al., 2010.

claim: mTOR is one of the downstream targets of ILR/TLRs signaling.
source: Furthermore, the signaling module containing the MyD88 adaptor protein, together with phosphorylated IRAK and TRAF6, which is downstream to both IL-1R and TLRs activation, is essential for PI3K recruitment and Akt activation, making mTOR one of the downstream targets of ILR/TLRs signaling (Gulen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gulen et al., 2010.

claim: Fine-tuning of MeCP2 expression is required for proper synapse function.
source: More importantly, our study shows for the first time that activation of IL-1R in neurons increases the levels of MeCP2, both in vitro and in vivo. Fine-tuning of MeCP2 expression is required for proper synapse function (reviewed in Na et al. [2013]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Na et al., 2013.

claim: Lack of expression of MeCP2 results in Rett syndrome characteristics including deceleration of body and head growth rate, problems in motor and speech capabilities, irregularities in motor activity and difficulties in breathing, and cognitive defects characteristic of an autism-spectrum disorder.
source: Indeed, lack of expression of MeCP2 results in deceleration of body and head growth rate, problems in motor and speech capabilities, irregularities in motor activity and difficulties in breathing, and also in cognitive defects characteristic of an autism-spectrum disorder (reviewed in Percy and Lane [2005]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Percy and Lane, 2005.

claim: Mouse models of MeCP2 duplication display a neurological phenotype including stereotyped and repetitive movements, epilepsy, spasticity, hypoactivity, and early death.
source: Mouse models of MeCP2 duplication display a neurological phenotype, stereotyped and repetitive movements, epilepsy, spasticity, hypoactivity, early death (Collins et al., 2004) and defects in dendritic arborization and spine morphology (Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2004 and Jiang et al., 2013.

claim: Sporadic mutations in the gene coding for MeCP2 result in Rett syndrome in humans.
source: In humans, sporadic mutations in the gene coding for MeCP2 results in Rett syndrome (Amir et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Amir et al., 1999.

claim: A double dosage of MeCP2 causes a severe developmental delay and mental retardation in humans.
source: while a double dosage of MeCP2 causes a severe developmental delay and mental retardation (Lubs et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lubs et al., 1999.

claim: MeCP2 can act as a transcriptional activator when interacting with CREB.
source: MeCP2 can act as a transcriptional activator (when interacting with CREB) but primarily functions as a transcriptional repressor associated with mSin3A and HDACs repressor complexes (Chahrour et al., 2008; Jones et al., 1998; Nan et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chahrour et al., 2008; Jones et al., 1998; Nan et al., 1998.

claim: MeCP2 primarily functions as a transcriptional repressor associated with mSin3A and HDACs repressor complexes.
source: MeCP2 can act as a transcriptional activator (when interacting with CREB) but primarily functions as a transcriptional repressor associated with mSin3A and HDACs repressor complexes (Chahrour et al., 2008; Jones et al., 1998; Nan et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chahrour et al., 2008; Jones et al., 1998; Nan et al., 1998.

claim: IL-1β is expressed at baseline levels in the healthy brain.
source: IL-1β is a fundamental factor of inflammatory responses in the brain. It is expressed at baseline levels in the healthy brain, and its expression increases following peripheral infection, surgery, or brain injury, as well as in neurodegenerative diseases (Rothwell and Luheshi, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rothwell and Luheshi, 2000.

claim: IL-1β expression increases following peripheral infection, surgery, or brain injury, as well as in neurodegenerative diseases.
source: IL-1β is a fundamental factor of inflammatory responses in the brain. It is expressed at baseline levels in the healthy brain, and its expression increases following peripheral infection, surgery, or brain injury, as well as in neurodegenerative diseases (Rothwell and Luheshi, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rothwell and Luheshi, 2000.

claim: Increases in IL-1β levels lead to cognitive decline, in particular in hippocampal-dependent tasks.
source: Increases in IL-1β levels lead to cognitive decline, in particular in hippocampal-dependent tasks (Rachal Pugh et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rachal Pugh et al., 2001.

claim: IL-1β overexpression for two weeks in an inducible transgenic mouse causes impairment in long-term contextual and spatial memory, without effects on short-term and non-hippocampal memory.
source: IL-1β overexpression for two weeks in an inducible transgenic mouse was found to cause impairment in long-term contextual and spatial memory, without effects on short-term and non-hippocampal memory (Hein et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hein et al., 2010.

claim: An increase in IL-1β levels due to Escherichia coli infection leads to defects in contextual fear conditioning.
source: An increase in IL-1β levels due to Escherichia coli infection leads to defects in contextual fear conditioning, with loss of memory prevented by IL1Ra (Barrientos et al., 2009; Frank et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barrientos et al., 2009 and Frank et al., 2010.

claim: Loss of memory due to E. coli infection is prevented by IL1Ra.
source: An increase in IL-1β levels due to Escherichia coli infection leads to defects in contextual fear conditioning, with loss of memory prevented by IL1Ra (Barrientos et al., 2009; Frank et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barrientos et al., 2009 and Frank et al., 2010.

claim: Recurrent infections occur in 70% of individuals affected by MeCP2 duplication syndrome.
source: Indeed, recurrent infections have been found to occur in 70% of individuals affected by MeCP2 duplication syndrome, which lead to further deterioration of the general and neurological status, being even fatal in some patients (van Esch et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to van Esch et al., 2012.

claim: In patients affected by cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS), the levels of IL-1β are fivefold higher than in healthy individuals.
source: Also, in patients affected by cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS), a group of rare autoinflammatory diseases with genetic basis, the levels of IL-1β are fivefold higher than in healthy individuals, leading to persistent unregulated systemic inflammation (Janssen et al., 2004; Lachmann et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Janssen et al., 2004 and Lachmann et al., 2009.

claim: Mental and hearing defects in CAPS are reversed following treatment with Anakinra.
source: Mental and hearing defects are reversed following treatment with Anakinra (Goldbach-Mansky, 2011; Goldbach-Mansky et al., 2006; Lepore et al., 2010; Miyamae et al., 2010; Neven et al., 2010) and with specific neutralization of IL-1β with canakinumab.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goldbach-Mansky, 2011; Goldbach-Mansky et al., 2006; Lepore et al., 2010; Miyamae et al., 2010; Neven et al., 2010.
